lessons.title: Certainty, strength and guideline labels
lessons.objective: Read a guideline's labels: the four GRADE certainty levels and what raises or lowers them, the difference between strength of recommendation and certainty, good practice points and other non-GRADE scales, and why a surrogate outcome is not enough.
lessons.closing: High, moderate, low or very low certainty, per outcome; trials start high and observational studies low. Strength and certainty are judged separately: “strong with ⊕” exists, as an exception that needs justifying. GPP and Level III are expert opinion. A semen parameter is not a live birth.

lessons.title: Reasoning with diagnostic tests
lessons.objective: Calculate and interpret sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and likelihood ratios, always start from the pre-test probability, and recognise when a test, including a commercial panel, cannot inform a decision.
lessons.closing: Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test; PPV and NPV depend on prevalence. Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR. Without a reference standard or an effect on important outcomes, the result cannot guide a decision.

lessons.title: Absolute risk, NNT and shared decision-making
lessons.objective: Translate relative effects into absolute effects and NNT, communicate risk as NICE recommends, and lead a shared decision, applying it to a typical integrative claim from clinic.
lessons.closing: Always ask “from what to what”. NNT = 1 / absolute difference, rounded up and with its time frame. Natural frequencies, the same denominator, both framings, and doing nothing on the table as an option.

items.title: GRADE certainty: four levels and where each design starts
items.core: GRADE rates the certainty (or quality) of evidence for each outcome at four levels: high, moderate, low and very low. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14]] High means great confidence that the true effect lies close to the estimate; very low means the true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimate. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.body:
It is rated per outcome and across the body of studies, not study by study: within the same trials, mortality may stay at high certainty while quality of life ends up lower. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] Randomised trials without important limitations start as high certainty and observational studies without special strengths or limitations as low; case series usually drop to very low. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] Expert opinion is not a level of evidence: it is an interpretation of evidence, and the type of studies behind it should be stated. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]

With the ROBINS-I tool, non-randomised studies may start as high certainty (and be rated down by up to three levels if a concern is extremely serious), but Cochrane notes that sound non-randomised studies are still usually graded low. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14]]
items.recall: What are the four GRADE certainty levels, and at what level do a randomised trial and an observational study start?
items.pearl: “There are studies” tells you nothing: ask what certainty the outcome your patient cares about has.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, table 5.1 and sections 5 and 5.1.1. Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 14, key points and section 14.2. Symbols suggested by GRADE: high ⨁⨁⨁⨁, moderate ⨁⨁⨁◯, low ⨁⨁◯◯, very low ⨁◯◯◯ (table 6.4).

items.title: What lowers and what raises certainty
items.core: Five factors can lower certainty by one or two levels: risk of bias, inconsistency of results, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] Three can raise it: a large magnitude of effect, a dose-response gradient, and all plausible confounding having reduced the observed effect. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14]]
items.body: It is not a mechanical sum: GRADE is not a quantitative system, each factor is a continuum that requires judgement, and its merit is that the judgement is explicit and transparent. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] If there are minor concerns about several factors, authors may rate down one level for one or two of them and explain it in a footnote. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] The factors for rating up apply mainly to non-randomised studies: with large effects and no obvious bias, they can reach moderate or even high certainty. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14]]
items.recall: Name the five reasons to rate certainty down and the three to rate it up.

rows.text: Randomised trials without important limitations: start at high certainty
Observational studies: start at low certainty
Rate down 1 or 2 levels: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias
Rate up: large effect (1 or 2 levels), dose-response (1), confounding that would reduce the effect (1)
Result for each outcome: high, moderate, low or very low

visual.alt: GRADE scheme: trials start at high certainty and observational studies at low; five factors lower it and three raise it, giving a final level per outcome.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, tables 5.2 and 5.3 and section 5.1. Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 14, section 14.2 (figure 14.2.a).

items.title: Strength of recommendation is not certainty of evidence
items.core: The strength of a recommendation reflects the panel's confidence that desirable effects outweigh undesirable ones (or vice versa), and GRADE judges it separately from certainty: there can be weak recommendations with high-certainty evidence and, exceptionally, strong ones with low or very low certainty: GRADE discourages the latter except in five paradigmatic situations (for example, possible benefit in a life-threatening situation or possible catastrophic harm). [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] A real example: ESHRE 2023 recommends ultrasound, preferably 3D, to exclude uterine anomalies in unexplained infertility as a strong recommendation with level ⊕. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
Besides certainty, strength depends on the balance of benefits and harms, on values and preferences (and how much they vary) and on resource use. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] Weak recommendations are also called conditional: most people would want the option but many would not, and each patient needs help to decide in line with her values; a strong recommendation means most people should receive it. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] ESHRE uses the same reading of “strong” and “conditional”, and automatically grades evidence as very low (+OOO) when there are no studies specific to unexplained infertility; so when you see “strong with ⊕”, read the justification to find out what the strength rests on. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Not even a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence is a dictate: GRADE warns that it should not be applied by rote to every patient. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.recall: Can a recommendation be strong with very low certainty? Give an ESHRE example.
items.pearl: Always read both labels: “strong” describes the panel's decision; the ⊕ symbols describe the studies.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, sections 1.2, 6.1, 6.1.1 and 6.1.2 and tables 6.1 and 6.2; section 6.3.2 and table 6.3 (five paradigmatic situations for a strong recommendation with low or very low certainty). ESHRE unexplained infertility 2023: rec. 10 in the list of recommendations (p. 8) and methods annex (p. 109), where evidence without specific studies is graded “very low (+OOO)”.

items.title: Labels that are not GRADE: GPP, NAMS levels and add-on phrases
items.core: In ESHRE guidelines, GPP (good practice point) marks a recommendation based mainly on expert opinion. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] NAMS 2022 grades with levels: I, good and consistent scientific evidence; II, limited or inconsistent evidence; III, mainly consensus and expert opinion. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body:
The 2023 ESHRE add-ons guideline uses four fixed phrases: “recommended” (applicable to most patients), “can be considered” (after a thorough discussion of benefits and risks and with close monitoring), “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” (may change with more evidence) and “not recommended” (for safety, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale; research settings only). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] Of its 42 recommendations, none could be based on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence; the rest rely on low-quality trials, observational data, professional experience or consensus (the guideline's abstract puts this at 95%, although 38 of 42 is 90%). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

GRADE warns that the use of letters and numbers varies widely between organisations and can confuse, so read each guideline's legend before comparing them. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.recall: What do GPP in ESHRE, Level III in NAMS and “can be considered” in the add-ons guideline mean?
items.pearl: A NAMS Level III or an ESHRE GPP is declared expert opinion: useful, but do not read it as if it were trial evidence.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE unexplained infertility 2023, footnote to the list of recommendations (p. 8). NAMS 2022, grading categories (p. 2). ESHRE add-ons 2023, table 1 (p. 3) and abstract (p. 1). GRADE Handbook 2013, section 6.3.2 and table 6.4.

items.title: Surrogate outcomes: a semen analysis is not a live birth
items.core: GRADE says surrogate outcomes should be used only when data on important outcomes are lacking, and using them usually lowers certainty by one or two levels for indirectness (two when the surrogate is far removed in the causal pathway). [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] The ESHRE add-ons guideline notes that many antioxidant studies used semen parameters or the DNA fragmentation index as surrogate success parameters rather than the pregnancy rate. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body: In the 2022 Cochrane review of antioxidants for male subfertility, the primary outcome was live birth, but of the 67 studies in the meta-analysis only 12 reported it. [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]] With those 12 trials, antioxidants may increase live births (OR 1.43; 95% CI 1.07 to 1.91; very low certainty), but when studies at high risk of bias were removed there was no longer evidence of an increase (Peto OR 1.22; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.75; 8 trials). [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]] ESHRE concludes that antioxidant therapy is not recommended in assisted reproduction treatment. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: Why is a study showing lower sperm DNA fragmentation not enough to recommend a supplement?
items.pearl: When you hear “improves semen quality” or “lowers fragmentation”, ask: and live births?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, sections 3.4 and 5.2.3. ESHRE add-ons 2023, antioxidants (pp. 27–28) and summary table (p. 31). Cochrane de Ligny et al. 2022, abstract: live birth OR 1.43 with very low certainty, and sensitivity analysis without the high risk-of-bias studies.

items.stem: A meta-analysis of well-conducted observational studies, with no large effect and no dose-response gradient, evaluates a supplement. Under the classic GRADE scheme (without the ROBINS-I tool), at what certainty does this evidence start?

options.text: High, because it is a meta-analysis
options.why: Pooling studies does not change the starting point: GRADE starts from the design of the included studies.

options.text: Moderate
options.why: Moderate is a possible result after rating up or down, not the starting point of an observational study.

options.text: Low
options.why: Correct: observational studies without special strengths or important limitations provide low-certainty evidence.

options.text: Very low, always
options.why: Very low applies, for example, to case series or to evidence rated down for limitations; it is not the starting point of a well-conducted observational study.

items.explanation: Trials without important limitations start as high certainty and observational studies as low. From there, certainty can fall for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or publication bias, and rise for a large effect, dose-response or confounding that would reduce the effect.

items.stem: In the 2023 ESHRE unexplained infertility guideline, ultrasound (preferably 3D) to exclude uterine anomalies is labelled “Strong ⊕”. How should this be read?

options.text: High-quality trials support it
options.why: A single ⊕ means very low certainty; “strong” refers to the panel's decision, not to the quality of the studies.

options.text: The panel is confident that benefits outweigh downsides for most patients, even though the certainty of evidence is very low
options.why: Correct: GRADE judges strength and certainty separately and, as an exception, allows strong recommendations with low or very low certainty.

options.text: It is a contradiction: with ⊕ only conditional recommendations are possible
options.why: It is not: separating strength from certainty is precisely GRADE's defining feature.

options.text: It is a good practice point (GPP)
options.why: In ESHRE guidelines, GPP is a different label, for recommendations based mainly on expert opinion, and carries no ⊕.

items.explanation: Strength depends on the balance of benefits and harms, on values and preferences and on resources, not only on certainty. That is why the same ESHRE list of recommendations contains “Strong ⊕”, “Strong ⊕⊕⊕” and “Conditional ⊕”. Even so, GRADE discourages strong recommendations with low or very low certainty except in specific situations: when you see “Strong ⊕”, read the justification.

items.stem: In the 2023 ESHRE add-ons guideline, what does the phrase “can be considered” imply?

options.text: It can be applied to most patients and adopted as policy
options.why: That is the definition of “recommended”.

options.text: It can be applied after a thorough discussion of benefits and risks, with close monitoring, follow-up and evaluation
options.why: Correct: this is the definition in table 1 of the guideline.

options.text: It should not be used routinely for now, although this may change with more evidence
options.why: That is the definition of “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”.

options.text: It should only be applied in research
options.why: That corresponds to “not recommended”, for safety, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale.

items.explanation: The add-ons guideline does not use GRADE strength but four fixed phrases. Moreover, of its 42 recommendations none rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence: the rest rely on low-quality trials, observational data, professional experience or consensus (38 of 42, 90%; the guideline's abstract says 95%).

items.stem: In the 2022 Cochrane review of antioxidants in subfertile men, live births may increase (OR 1.43; 95% CI 1.07 to 1.91; 12 trials; very low certainty). Without the studies at high risk of bias, the result is Peto OR 1.22 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.75). Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Antioxidants clearly increase live births
options.why: Certainty is very low, and the increase is no longer seen when only the lower risk-of-bias studies remain.

options.text: The benefit is not robust: it depends on studies at high risk of bias, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidants in assisted reproduction
options.why: Correct: the sensitivity analysis shows no increase, and the authors describe the evidence as inconclusive.

options.text: It proves that antioxidants have no effect at all
options.why: The authors conclude that the evidence is inconclusive, not that the effect is zero.

options.text: Semen improvement should guide the decision, as it is more reliable
options.why: Semen parameters are a surrogate outcome; the one that matters to the couple is live birth.

items.explanation: When an effect disappears after removing the studies at highest risk of bias, the overall result is probably inflated. Add the surrogate outcomes of many studies and the ESHRE recommendation: not recommended in assisted reproduction.

items.title: Sensitivity and specificity: properties of the test
items.core: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease (by the reference standard) who test positive; specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]] In a teaching example of D-dimer against perfusion scanning, 7 of 10 people with embolism test positive (sensitivity 70%) and 77 of 90 without embolism test negative (specificity 85.6%). [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]]
items.body:
A highly sensitive test is hardly ever negative in someone with the disease, so a negative result almost rules it out (SnNOut); a highly specific test is hardly ever positive in someone without it, so a positive result almost rules it in (SpPIn). [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]] Their clinical limitation is that they start from knowing who is ill; in clinic you need the opposite, the probability of disease given a result. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]]

All of this requires a reference standard: STARD 2015 asks for it to be described in detail, its choice justified, and the index test cross-tabulated against it. [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]]
items.recall: Define sensitivity and specificity and explain SnNOut and SpPIn.
items.pearl: Without a reference standard there is no sensitivity or specificity to calculate.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Ranganathan and Aggarwal 2018, part 1 (hypothetical teaching example). STARD 2015, items 10b, 11 and 23.

items.title: Predictive values: they depend on whom you test
items.core: PPV is the probability of having the disease with a positive test and NPV the probability of not having it with a negative test; unlike sensitivity and specificity, they depend heavily on the prevalence in the tested population. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]] With the same test (sensitivity 70%, specificity 85.6%), PPV is 7/150 = 4.7% at 1% prevalence, 70/200 = 35.0% at 10% and 210/311 = 67.5% at 30%. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]]
items.body: So even a test with good sensitivity and specificity has a low PPV when the pre-test probability is low, and the authors advise applying tests to people with a high pre-test probability based on symptoms and signs. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]] This often happens when a test becomes cheaper and starts being used indiscriminately in people with a low likelihood of disease. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]]
items.recall: What happens to a test's PPV when you use it in a low-prevalence population?
items.pearl: At 1% prevalence, only 7 of every 150 positives had the disease.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Ranganathan and Aggarwal 2018, part 1, tables 3a–3c (figures in the text). NPV is 99.6%, 96.2% and 86.9% at prevalences of 1%, 10% and 30%. Hypothetical example.

items.title: Likelihood ratios: from pre-test to post-test probability
items.core: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) and LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity; they do not change with prevalence (in the D-dimer example, LR+ 4.85 and LR− 0.35 at prevalences of 1%, 10% and 30%). [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]] To use them: post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR, with odds = probability / (1 − probability) and probability = odds / (1 + odds). [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]]
items.body:
An LR of 1.0 adds nothing; the further it moves from 1, the more it discriminates, and LRs > 10 or < 0.1 are very useful to establish or exclude a diagnosis. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]] The same positive D-dimer leaves a probability of embolism of about 67% when the pre-test probability was 30%, and 5% when it was 1%; recalculated (0.43 × 4.85 ≈ 2.08 odds; the article gives 2.04), it is 67.5%, the same value as the PPV at that prevalence. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]]

Limitations: an LR is only as reliable as the studies it comes from, the pre-test probability must be individualised, and there is no consensus on how to combine the LRs of several tests. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]]
items.recall: Write the formulas for LR+ and LR− and how to go from pre-test to post-test probability.
items.pearl: Before ordering a test, estimate the pre-test probability: without it the result cannot be interpreted.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Ranganathan and Aggarwal 2018, part 2 (hypothetical example): LR+ = (7/10)/(13/90) = 4.85; LR− = (3/10)/(77/90) = 0.35. Worked numerical exercise in question 7.

items.title: Accuracy is not usefulness: does the result change anything for the patient?
items.core: GRADE is blunt: if a test fails to improve patient-important outcomes there is no reason to use it, whatever its accuracy; the best design to evaluate it is a trial that randomises diagnostic strategies and measures mortality, morbidity, symptoms, quality of life and resource use. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] When only accuracy studies exist, accuracy acts as a surrogate outcome, and you must ask what will happen to those the test labels as diseased and as healthy under the best available management. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.body: Accuracy studies are also at risk of bias: if not all tested patients are analysed, or if only healthy controls are included, the accuracy estimates may not reflect performance in practice. [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]] That is why STARD 2015 asks, among its 30 items, for the intended use and clinical role of the test, how participants were identified and whether they were a consecutive, random or convenience series, the positivity cut-offs and whether they were pre-specified, and the estimates with their precision (for example, 95% CIs). [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]]
items.recall: Why might an accurate test still not be indicated?
items.pearl: For every test, ask before ordering it: what will I do differently with each possible result?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, ch. 7 (diagnostic tests, figure 1 and sections 7.3 and 7.4). STARD 2015, items 3, 7, 9, 12a, 24, 26 and 27.

items.title: Commercial panels without demonstrated validity
items.core: The 2025 international consensus on microbiome testing considers the evidence insufficient to widely recommend routine use in clinical practice (90% agreement) and discourages patients from requesting tests without a clinical recommendation (80.4%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] It adds that there is generally not enough information to report strict healthy reference ranges for species abundance (90%), discourages the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), and finds insufficient evidence to include any dysbiosis index (90%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.body: The same logic applies to any commercial panel: accuracy is measured against a reference standard in a published study, such as STARD describes; without one there is no sensitivity, specificity or LR with which to interpret the result. [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]] [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]] And even with good accuracy, if the result does not improve important outcomes there is no reason to order it. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] The same consensus discourages the test provider from giving any post-test therapeutic advice (98%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.recall: What would a commercial panel have to demonstrate before its result could help you decide?
items.pearl: Before interpreting a panel, ask for two things: the accuracy study against a reference standard and the study showing it changes outcomes.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: Porcari et al. 2025, table 1: statements 6, 26, 27, 28, 30 and 32 (% Delphi agreement; no GRADE because of their conceptual content). GRADE Handbook 2013, ch. 7. STARD 2015.

items.stem: In a teaching example, a test is compared with the reference standard in 100 people: of the 10 with the disease, 7 test positive; of the 90 without it, 77 test negative. What are the sensitivity and specificity?

options.text: Sensitivity 70% and specificity 85.6%
Sensitivity 35% and specificity 96%
options.why: These are the PPV (7 of 20 positives = 35%) and the NPV (77 of 80 negatives = 96%), not sensitivity and specificity.

options.text: Sensitivity 85.6% and specificity 70%
options.why: They are swapped: sensitivity is calculated in the diseased and specificity in the non-diseased.

options.text: Sensitivity 7% and specificity 77%
options.why: These are counts out of the total of 100, not proportions within each group.

items.explanation: Sensitivity = true positives / all diseased; specificity = true negatives / all non-diseased. Predictive values use a different denominator: all positives or all negatives.

items.stem: The same test (sensitivity 70%, specificity 85.6%) is applied to 1000 people at 1% prevalence: there are 150 positives, of whom 7 have the disease. What is the PPV and what does it teach?

options.text: 4.7%: with a low pre-test probability, the vast majority of positives are false positives
options.why: Correct: 7/150 = 4.7%; 143 of the 150 positives do not have the disease.

options.text: 70%, because PPV equals sensitivity
options.why: Sensitivity is calculated among the diseased; PPV among those who test positive.

options.text: 35%, because PPV is a fixed property of the test
options.why: 35% was the PPV at 10% prevalence; PPV changes with prevalence.
That is the NPV in this scenario (847/850), not the PPV.

items.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity do not change, but PPV falls from 67.5% (30% prevalence) to 35.0% (10%) and 4.7% (1%). Testing people with a low pre-test probability fills the clinic with false positives.

items.stem: A test has 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity (numerical exercise). Your patient has a 10% pre-test probability and the result is positive. What is the post-test probability?

options.why: That would be the post-test probability if the pre-test probability were 50% (odds 1 × 9 = 9; 9/10 = 90%); equating it with sensitivity ignores the pre-test probability.
Correct: LR+ = 0.9/(1 − 0.9) = 9; pre-test odds = 0.1/0.9 = 1/9; post-test odds = 1/9 × 9 = 1; probability = 1/(1 + 1) = 50%.
Multiplying sensitivity by specificity (0.9 × 0.9) is meaningless here; you multiply the pre-test odds by the LR+.
Staying at 10% would imply an LR of 1; an LR+ of 9 does change the probability.

items.explanation: The same positive result with LR+ 9 takes you to 50% if the pre-test probability was 10% and to 90% if it was 50%. The test does not deliver “the diagnosis”: it updates the probability you already had.

items.stem: A patient brings a commercial stool panel with a high “dysbiosis index” and asks you to treat it. The laboratory publishes no study against a reference standard. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat, because the index is out of range
options.why: The 2025 consensus finds insufficient evidence to include dysbiosis indices or strict healthy reference ranges.

options.text: Repeat the same panel to confirm it
options.why: Repeating a test of unknown validity does not make it valid: it still has no known sensitivity, specificity or LR.

options.text: Explain that without demonstrated accuracy or an effect on outcomes the result cannot inform the decision, and return to her clinical problem
options.why: Correct: without a reference standard there is no accuracy to interpret, and GRADE adds that a test that does not improve outcomes has no reason to be used.

options.text: Order another brand's panel and compare
options.why: Two unvalidated tests do not make a reference standard.

items.explanation: The 2025 consensus does not recommend routine microbiome testing, and discourages ordering it without a clinical recommendation and providers giving therapeutic advice. The useful question is what clinical problem the patient has and what evidence exists for it.

items.title: Relative versus absolute risk
items.core: Going from a 4% to a 3% risk is a 25% relative reduction and a 1 percentage point absolute reduction: the same benefit, but the relative figure makes prescribing more tempting. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] NAMS defines relative risk as the ratio of event rates in two groups and absolute risk as their difference, and considers absolute risk more useful for conveying risks and benefits in clinic. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body: Relative effects tend to be more stable across risk groups than absolute ones, so the absolute benefit depends on the baseline risk: in atrial fibrillation, warfarin prevents about 70 strokes a year per 1000 high-risk patients (about 120 strokes per 1000 a year) and only 12 in low-risk patients (about 20 per 1000). [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] NICE NG197 recommends absolute rather than relative risk: say the risk rises from 1 in 1000 to 2 in 1000, not that it doubles. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] NAMS adds that very small effects may be less clinically relevant, particularly for rare outcomes (Level I). [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.recall: A risk falls from 4% to 3%: what are the relative and the absolute reductions?
items.pearl: When you read “cuts risk by 50%”, ask: from what to what, and over what time?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 15, sections 15.4.1 and 15.4.3. NAMS 2022, “Explaining hormone therapy risk” and key points (p. 2). NICE NG197, rec. 1.4.7 (p. 15).

items.title: Number needed to treat (NNT)
items.core: The NNT is the expected number of people who need to receive the experimental rather than the comparator intervention for one additional person to incur or avoid an event over a given time. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] It is computed as 1 divided by the absolute value of the risk difference and always rounded up: with a difference of −0.12 the NNT is 9, and with −0.22 it is 5. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]]
items.body: If the meta-analysis gives an RR, a baseline risk has to be assumed: with RR 0.92 and an assumed comparator risk of 0.3 (300 per 1000), the effect is 24 fewer events per 1000 and the NNT is 42. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] The NNT is comparative (against a specific comparator), it is an expected value (an NNT of 10 does not mean one event in every group of 10), and it must come with its time frame. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] Cochrane advises against the phrase “number needed to harm” and prefers NNTB and NNTH, for an additional beneficial or harmful outcome. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]]
items.recall: How is the NNT calculated from a risk difference, and which way is it rounded?
items.pearl: An NNT without a comparator, a baseline risk and a time frame cannot be interpreted.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 15, sections 15.4.2, 15.4.4, 15.4.4.1 and 15.4.4.2. The chapter's formulas are images that were not extracted: their text description and worked examples were used (1/0.12 = 8.3 → 9; 1/0.22 = 4.5 → 5; 1/0.024 = 41.7 → 42).

items.title: Shared decision-making step by step (NICE NG197)
items.core: NICE defines shared decision making as a collaborative process in which a person and their healthcare professional work together to reach a joint decision about care. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] When discussing tests or treatments, it recommends explaining the aims of each option, openly discussing the risks, benefits and consequences of each (including no treatment or no change), clarifying what the person hopes to gain and discussing any misconceptions. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]]
items.body:
The NG197 steps: agree an agenda and say how long the discussion will last (1.2.7); give information in manageable chunks and check understanding, for example with teach back (1.2.11); give the time needed (1.2.12); accept that the person may weigh risks and benefits differently from the professional (1.2.13); make a joint decision and agree when to review it (1.2.14); summarise at the end what has been decided and what happens next (1.2.15); and explain that they can change their mind at any time (1.2.16). [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] Decision aids should only be used if they are quality assured, reflect evidence-based best practice and are relevant to that decision and setting. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]]

GRADE notes that weak recommendations require more time for shared decision making, because not everyone is best served by the same option. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.recall: List the NICE NG197 steps for shared decision making.
items.pearl: “Doing nothing” is always an option to put on the table, with its numbers.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG197 (2021): definition (p. 5), recs 1.2.7–1.2.16 (pp. 10–12) and 1.3.1–1.3.2 (p. 13). GRADE Handbook 2013, section 6.1.2.

items.title: Communicating numbers as NICE recommends
items.core: NICE NG197 recommends using numerical data when available, because people interpret words such as “rare” or “common” differently, and doing so with absolute risk, with natural frequencies (10 in 100) rather than percentages, and with the same denominator when comparing (7 in 100 against 20 in 100, not 1 in 14 against 1 in 5). [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]]
items.body: In addition: present risk over a defined time period (if 100 people are treated for 1 year, 10 will have a given side effect), use positive and negative framing together (it works for 97 in 100 and does not work for 3 in 100), and combine numbers with pictograms. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] Information should be personalised as far as possible, making clear how it applies to the person and how much uncertainty it carries. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] Cochrane agrees that natural frequencies are the way of expressing absolute differences that healthcare consumers understand best. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]]
items.recall: According to NICE, how should you present a risk to a patient?
items.pearl: Say “out of 100 women in your situation…”, not “30% more”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG197, recs 1.4.2 and 1.4.5–1.4.11 (pp. 14–15). Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 15, section 15.4.3.

items.stem: A meta-analysis gives an RR of 0.92 for an event; in your patients the baseline risk is 30% (300 per 1000). What are the absolute effect and the NNT?

options.text: 24 fewer per 1000; NNT 42
8 fewer per 100; NNT 13
options.why: It confuses the relative reduction (8%) with the absolute one; the absolute reduction is 8% of a 30% risk, that is, 2.4 points.

options.text: 24 fewer per 1000; NNT 41
options.why: By convention the NNT is always rounded up: 41.7 becomes 42.

options.text: An NNT cannot be calculated from an RR
options.why: It can, if a baseline risk is assumed; Cochrane advises doing so for a range of baseline risks.

items.explanation: From RR to NNT: risk with the intervention = baseline risk × RR; difference = baseline risk − risk with the intervention; NNT = 1 / difference, rounded up. With a different baseline risk, the same RR gives a different NNT.

items.stem: A treatment raises a side effect from 1 to 2 in every 1000 people. According to NICE NG197, how do you communicate it?

options.text: “This treatment doubles the risk”
options.why: That is relative risk; NICE recommends absolute rather than relative risk.

options.text: “The risk goes from 1 in 1000 to 2 in 1000 people”
options.why: Correct: absolute risk, in natural frequencies and with the same denominator; it is the example in recommendation 1.4.7.

options.text: “The risk increases by 100%”
options.why: It is still relative risk, and in a percentage rather than natural frequencies.

options.text: “It is a rare risk, don't worry”
options.why: NICE warns that words such as “rare” are interpreted differently and asks for numbers when available.

items.explanation: NG197: absolute risk, natural frequencies, the same denominator, a defined time period, and positive and negative framing. Here: 999 in 1000 without the side effect untreated, against 998 in 1000 treated.

items.stem: A study announces that an intervention “cuts risk by 25%”: the risk went from 4% to 3%. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The absolute reduction is 25%
options.why: 25% is the relative reduction (1 of 4); the absolute reduction is the difference, 1 point.

options.text: The relative reduction is 25% and the absolute reduction 1 percentage point (NNT 100)
options.why: Correct: (4 − 3)/4 = 25% relative; 4 − 3 = 1 point absolute; 1/0.01 = 100.

options.text: The absolute reduction is 3%
options.why: 3% is the final risk, not the difference between groups.

options.text: Relative and absolute coincide if the study is large
options.why: Study size does not change the relationship between the two measures: the absolute one depends on the baseline risk.

items.explanation: It is the Cochrane example: the same benefit sounds larger in relative terms (“25%”) than in absolute terms (“1 point”). To decide and to explain, use the absolute figure and its NNT.

items.title: Case: Julia and an antioxidant “for fragmentation”

steps.text: Julia (fictional case), 35, is about to start IVF with her partner, Adrián, who has raised sperm DNA fragmentation. She brings a website claiming that an antioxidant blend “cuts fragmentation by 40%” (fictional claim). The first thing you check is the outcome: fragmentation is a surrogate, and GRADE asks you to look for the important outcome, here live birth; ESHRE notes that many antioxidant studies used exactly these surrogates. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

You look for the best evidence on live births: the 2022 Cochrane review finds an OR of 1.43 with very low certainty, which no longer shows an increase once the studies at high risk of bias are removed, and the ESHRE add-ons guideline concludes that antioxidants are not recommended in assisted reproduction. [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

The same website offers an “oxidative stress panel” to adjust the dose. You find no study comparing it with a reference standard or showing that it changes outcomes, so its accuracy is unknown and its result cannot guide the decision. [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]] [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]

You discuss it with Julia and Adrián following NICE NG197: the options, including taking nothing, in natural frequencies and with their uncertainty. According to the Cochrane review, if 16 in 100 couples have a live birth without antioxidants, with antioxidants it would be between 17 and 27, with very low certainty and no demonstrated increase when only studies at lower risk of bias are kept; and mild gastrointestinal discomfort would go from 2 in 100 to between 2 and 7 (low certainty). They decide not to take it and agree to review the decision if better evidence appears. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]]

bossuyt-2015-stard.title: STARD 2015: an updated list of essential items for reporting diagnostic accuracy studies
bossuyt-2015-stard.authors: Bossuyt PM, Reitsma JB, Bruns DE, Gatsonis CA, Glasziou PP, Irwig L, Lijmer JG, Moher D, Rennie D, de Vet HC, Kressel HY, Rifai N, Golub RM, Altman DG, Hooft L, Korevaar DA, Cohen JF; STARD Group
bossuyt-2015-stard.population: Authors, editors and readers of diagnostic accuracy studies (an index test against a reference standard).
bossuyt-2015-stard.finding: List of 30 essential items for reporting a diagnostic accuracy study, including the intended use and clinical role of the test, how participants were identified, the reference standard, positivity cut-offs, blinding, the cross tabulation of results against the reference standard, and the precision of estimates. These studies are at risk of bias: if not all tested patients are analysed, or if only healthy controls are included, the accuracy estimates may not reflect the test's real performance.
bossuyt-2015-stard.limitations: Full text read (BMJ 2015;351:h5527, Europe PMC version PMC4623764). It is a reporting guideline, not a risk-of-bias tool or a clinical guideline.

cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.title: Chapter 14: Completing ‘Summary of findings’ tables and grading the certainty of the evidence. Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions version 6.5
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.authors: Schünemann HJ, Higgins JP, Vist GE, Glasziou P, Akl EA, Skoetz N, Guyatt GH
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.population: Authors and readers of Cochrane intervention reviews: summary of findings tables and certainty assessment with GRADE.
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.finding: Cochrane adopts GRADE: four certainty levels for each outcome (high, moderate, low, very low), five domains for rating down (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias) and, for non-randomised and rarely randomised studies, three domains for rating up. Sound non-randomised studies are usually graded low; with large effects and no obvious bias they may be rated moderate or even high.
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.limitations: Web text of the chapter read (last updated August 2023, in version 6.5, 2024). Figures were read as text; some formulas and images were not extracted.

cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.title: Chapter 15: Interpreting results and drawing conclusions. Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions version 6.5
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.authors: Schünemann HJ, Vist GE, Higgins JP, Santesso N, Deeks JJ, Glasziou P, Akl EA, Guyatt GH
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.population: Authors and readers of Cochrane reviews: interpreting confidence intervals, relative and absolute measures, number needed to treat and conclusions.
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.finding: A risk reduction from 4% to 3% is a 25% relative reduction and a 1 percentage point absolute reduction; a risk ratio of 0.75 equals a 25% relative risk reduction. The NNT is the expected number of people who need to receive the experimental rather than the comparator intervention for one additional person to incur or avoid an event over a given time; it is computed from the absolute value of the risk difference and rounded up (risk difference −0.12: NNT 9; −0.22: NNT 5). With RR 0.92 and an assumed comparator risk of 0.3, the effect is 24 fewer per 1000 and the NNT is 42. Relative effects are more stable across risk groups than absolute ones, so absolute benefit should be expressed for each baseline risk; natural frequencies are understood best.
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.limitations: Web text of the chapter read (last updated August 2023, in version 6.5, 2024). The formulas are images and were not extracted: only the chapter's text description and its own numerical examples were used.

deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.authors: de Ligny W, Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Jordan V, Fleischer K, de Bruin JP, Showell MG
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.population: 90 RCTs, 10,303 subfertile men (aged 18–65) of couples attending fertility clinics, some undergoing assisted reproduction; 20 different oral antioxidants. Excluded men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters. Search to 15 Feb 2021. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;5:CD007411.
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.finding: Live birth: OR 1.43 (95% CI 1.07–1.91; 12 RCTs; 1283 men; very low certainty; 246 live births); with a 16% baseline, 17–27% with antioxidants. Excluding high risk-of-bias studies: no evidence of increase (Peto OR 1.22; 95% CI 0.85–1.75; 8 RCTs; 827 men). Clinical pregnancy: OR 1.89 (1.45–2.47; 20 RCTs; 1706 men; low certainty). Miscarriage: no difference (OR 1.46; 0.75–2.83; 6 RCTs; very low certainty). Mild gastrointestinal discomfort: OR 2.70 (1.46–4.99; 16 RCTs; low certainty). Only 20 of 67 meta-analysed studies reported clinical pregnancy and 12 live birth. Authors' conclusion: overall evidence inconclusive owing to serious risk of bias and imprecision.
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.limitations: Full abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 35506389; text saved in the source library), including the sensitivity analysis and the authors’ conclusions; ESHRE add-ons 2023 reproduces the live-birth, miscarriage and gastrointestinal figures. Full text, GRADE tables and semen-parameter results not read. Antioxidants and doses highly heterogeneous; excluded men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters.

eshre-2023-addons.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine
eshre-2023-addons.authors: ESHRE Add-ons Working Group; Lundin K, Bentzen JG, Bozdag G, Ebner T, Harper J, Le Clef N, Moffett A, Norcross S, Polyzos NP, Rautakallio-Hokkanen S, Sfontouris I, Sermon K, Vermeulen N, Pinborg A
eshre-2023-addons.population: Patients undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART); Hum Reprod 2023 (ESHRE Pages).
eshre-2023-addons.finding: 42 recommendations using its own four-phrase scale (recommended; can be considered; currently not recommended for routine clinical use; not recommended). Peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK-cell testing: not recommended. Screening hysteroscopy: currently not recommended for routine clinical use (can be considered in recurrent implantation failure). Sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping: currently not recommended for routine clinical use. ICSI for non-male factor infertility: not recommended.
eshre-2023-addons.limitations: Full text read (UCL Discovery open-access copy of the advance online version); the wording of every cited recommendation and the scale-definition table were checked verbatim. Good practice recommendations based on review and consensus, not a GRADE guideline: no recommendation rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence. ART population, not specifically unexplained infertility.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

grade-2013-handbook.title: GRADE Handbook: handbook for grading the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations using the GRADE approach
grade-2013-handbook.authors: Schünemann H, Brożek J, Guyatt G, Oxman A (editors); GRADE Working Group
grade-2013-handbook.population: Methods handbook for authors of systematic reviews, guidelines and health technology assessments who use GRADE: intervention and diagnostic test questions.
grade-2013-handbook.finding: Four levels of quality (certainty) of evidence: high, moderate, low and very low (table 5.1). Randomised trials without important limitations start as high quality and observational studies as low; five factors can lower it by 1 or 2 levels (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias) and three can raise it (large effect, dose-response gradient, residual confounding that would reduce the effect). The strength of a recommendation (strong or weak/conditional) is judged separately from quality: weak recommendations with high-quality evidence and strong ones with low or very low quality are both possible. Surrogate outcomes are used only when data on important outcomes are lacking and usually lower quality by 1 or 2 levels for indirectness. If a test fails to improve patient-important outcomes there is no reason to use it, whatever its accuracy.
grade-2013-handbook.limitations: Full web text read (version updated October 2013). The site itself warns that the handbook is being replaced by the GRADE Book (available since 2024 at book.gradepro.org) and will be phased out; sections 1, 2, 3, 5 (including 5.2) and 8 are marked as rewritten there. The definitions of certainty levels and of the factors for rating down or up match chapter 14 of the Cochrane Handbook (2024); those on strength of recommendation, surrogate outcomes, expert opinion and diagnostic tests come from this handbook only. It says “quality” where newer texts say “certainty”.

nams-2022-hormone-therapy.title: The 2022 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.authors: The 2022 Hormone Therapy Position Statement Advisory Panel of The North American Menopause Society (now The Menopause Society); Faubion SS (lead), Crandall CJ, Davis L, El Khoudary SR, Hodis HN, Lobo RA, Maki PM, Manson JE, Pinkerton JV, Santoro NF, Shifren JL, Shufelt CL, Thurston RC, Wolfman W
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.population: Perimenopausal and postmenopausal women considering hormone therapy, in the United States context (FDA indications). Position statement by an expert panel of The North American Menopause Society, approved by its Board of Trustees; Menopause 2022;29(7):767-794. Updates the 2017 statement.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.finding: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, and prevents bone loss and fracture. In women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset without contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favourable; when started after 60 or more than 10 years from menopause it appears less favourable because of greater absolute risks of coronary heart disease, stroke, venous thromboembolism and dementia. Women with a uterus need adequate progestogen. It does not need to be routinely stopped at 60–65. Compounded “bioidentical” hormones raise safety concerns, and saliva or urine testing to set the dose is unreliable.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.limitations: Full PDF (28 pp.) read on the society's website. It is a consensus position statement, not a guideline with a formal systematic review: the “Key points” carry levels I (good and consistent evidence), II (limited or inconsistent) and III (consensus and expert opinion), with no separate strength grade. Much of the risk data comes from the WHI trials (oral conjugated equine estrogens and medroxyprogesterone acetate). US regulatory context. It was the current version as of 14-10-2026 (the society has published no later one).

nice-2021-ng197.title: Shared decision making. NICE guideline NG197
nice-2021-ng197.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2021-ng197.population: People using healthcare services and the professionals and organisations of the English health service (NHS); all decisions about tests, treatments and interventions.
nice-2021-ng197.finding: Shared decision making is a collaborative process in which a person and their healthcare professional work together to reach a joint decision. In practice: agree an agenda, explain the aims of each option, discuss openly the risks, benefits and consequences of each (including no treatment or no change), clarify what the person hopes to gain, give information in chunks and check understanding (teach back), give time, accept that their views may differ from the professional's, make a joint decision and agree when to review it, and make clear they can change their mind (1.2.7–1.2.16). To communicate risk: absolute rather than relative risk, natural frequencies, the same denominator, a defined time period and both positive and negative framing (1.4.5–1.4.11).
nice-2021-ng197.limitations: Full PDF read (32 pp., published 17 June 2021). It is an English health-service guideline: several recommendations are organisational (section 1.1) and are not cited here. The accompanying evidence reviews were not read.

porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.title: International consensus statement on microbiome testing in clinical practice
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.authors: Porcari S, Mullish BH, Asnicar F, Ng SC, Zhao L, Hansen R, O'Toole PW, Raes J, Hold G, Putignani L, et al.; Cammarota G, Gasbarrini A, Ianiro G
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.population: Microbiome testing (mainly gut) in clinical practice; 69 experts from 18 countries, Delphi consensus. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025;10(2):154-167.
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.finding: There is insufficient evidence to widely recommend routine microbiome testing (90%). It discourages direct patient requests without a clinical recommendation (80.4%), therapeutic advice from the provider (98%), the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), dysbiosis indices (90%) and strict healthy reference ranges (90%). Multiplex PCR and cultures are not microbiome testing (90%); vaginal samples should be processed according to existing evidence and indications (97.5%).
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.limitations: The accepted author manuscript on PMC (PMC12343204) was read, not the typeset version; appendices not included. Expert-opinion statements (Delphi, ≥ 80% threshold), not GRADE recommendations; focused on the gut microbiome rather than vaginal or endometrial microbiome.

ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1.title: Common pitfalls in statistical analysis: Understanding the properties of diagnostic tests - Part 1
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1.population: Teaching statistics article for clinicians (Perspect Clin Res 2018;9(1):40-43); hypothetical example of D-dimer against perfusion scanning in pulmonary embolism.
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1.finding: Sensitivity: proportion of people with the disease (by the reference standard) who test positive (7/10 = 70% in the example); specificity: proportion without the disease who test negative (77/90 = 85.6%). PPV and NPV: probability of disease with a positive test (7/20 = 35%) or of no disease with a negative test (77/80 = 96%). Sensitivity and specificity are usually not influenced by prevalence; predictive values are: at 1% prevalence the PPV falls to 7/150 = 4.7% and the NPV is 847/850 = 99.6%. A test is best applied to people with a high pre-test probability.
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1.limitations: Full text read (Europe PMC, PMC5799952). The tables were not extracted, but every figure used appears in the text. Hypothetical teaching example, not clinical D-dimer data.

ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2.title: Understanding the properties of diagnostic tests - Part 2: Likelihood ratios
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2.population: Teaching statistics article for clinicians (Perspect Clin Res 2018;9(2):99-102); continues the hypothetical D-dimer example.
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2.finding: LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity. In the example, LR+ = (7/10)/(13/90) = 4.85 and LR− = (3/10)/(77/90) = 0.35, unchanged at prevalences of 1%, 10% and 30%. An LR of 1.0 changes nothing; LRs > 10 or < 0.1 are very useful to rule in or rule out. Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR; odds = probability/(1 − probability); probability = odds/(1 + odds). With a positive D-dimer, the post-test probability is 67% when the pre-test probability is 30% and 5% when it is 1%. The accuracy of LRs depends on the quality of the studies they come from.
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2.limitations: Full text read (Europe PMC, PMC5950618). The tables were not extracted; the figures used appear in the text. Hypothetical teaching example.
